title: The parables, looking back
hook: a sower, a lost coin, a mustard seed: stories that still work on you
tomorrow: what do you do with news you can't explain yet?

segments.voice: Yesterday, four forties, and the first day of the summit: the last climb. Today, from up here, the stories Jesus told, and an old argument about them.
screen: `THE LAST CLIMB.` → `THE STORIES, FROM UP HERE.`

segments.voice: Ask a yes-or-no question and get a story about a farmer back. It can feel like help, or like a dodge. Jesus answered this way all the time: a sower, a woman sweeping for one lost coin, a mustard seed. So were the parables meant to make things plain, or to keep them hidden? Christians have read them both ways, and each side has a verse.
screen: `A QUESTION, ANSWERED WITH A STORY.` → `A SOWER, A COIN, A SEED.` → `PLAIN, OR HIDDEN?`

segments.voice: View one: the stories are a kindness. Mark says, “And with many such parables spake he the word unto them, as they were able to hear it.” As they were able. A parable meets a listener where they are: farmers hear about seed, a woman with ten coins hears about the one she lost. Nobody needs training to follow it. View two: the stories also sift. When his friends ask why he talks this way, Jesus says that for those outside, everything comes in parables, “That seeing they may see, and not perceive.” He's echoing the prophet Isaiah. On this reading a parable never forces itself on anyone; it waits for whoever wants it enough to ask. Both sides have a fair case. The first can point to Mark's note that the common people heard him gladly. The second can point to how often even his friends were lost. And here's the detail both keep, worth telling a friend tonight: the explanation went to whoever came back. Mark says, “when they were alone, he expounded all things to his disciples.” The sower is a story about this very thing. The same seed falls on four kinds of ground, and Jesus ends, “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.” Looking back from near the top, a parable heard long ago may say something new now. The seed didn't change. The ground did.
screen: `VIEW ONE: AS THEY WERE ABLE.` · `VIEW TWO: SEEING, NOT PERCEIVING.` · `BOTH: HE EXPLAINED TO THOSE WHO ASKED.` · `THE SAME SEED, NEW GROUND.` · then, large: `STORIES STILL WORKING.`

segments.voice: Choose the parable that has stayed with you longest, and tell it out loud in your own words, start to finish, slowly. Notice which part catches now; it may not be the part that caught at first. If you pray, ask what it's still saying.
The parables. The short stories Jesus told, a sower, a coin, a seed, plain to some, waiting for others, and heard anew as the listener changes.
Pocket this one: stories still working, and the meaning goes to whoever comes back and asks. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians hear the parables read in worship, study them in groups, and return to them over a lifetime; some find a different detail stands out each time.

fork.setup: a friend says, "parables are just Jesus being clear with simple stories." give the best case for the other view.
options: parables were only meant for children; adults got plain teaching.
in Mark, Jesus says parables let some see and not perceive; they wait for those who ask.
Jesus spoke in riddles so that nobody could ever understand him.
fork.reveal: Mark 4 holds both: 'as they were able to hear it', and 'seeing they may see, and not perceive'. both views agree the explanation went to those who came back.

original.note: the Greek word for 'parable', as in Mark 4:33: something set alongside.

trapdoor: what you thought: a parable is a simple story with one moral.
what it means: a story that meets some listeners at once and waits for others to ask.
what a scholar hears: Mark 4 holds both 'as they were able to hear it' (4:33) and 'seeing they may see, and not perceive' (4:12, echoing Isaiah 6:9–10).
guess: short stories of Jesus that keep on teaching
fables that each end with a stated moral
sayings of the prophets set to music

chat.says: asked Pop if i should go. he told me a story about a farmer throwing seed everywhere. why not answer??
options: Maybe he wants you to find it. Go back and ask what he meant; that's how parables work.
He's dodging. A story like that is only a gentler way of saying no.
It's a farming story. He means stay home, where your roots are planted.
chat.meaning: In Mark, a parable meets listeners where they are, and the explanation goes to whoever comes back and asks. Pop's story is an invitation.
